Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Car Similarity: Similar cars, Crowding: Crowded places
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Face Hiding: cover face with hands

Vignette:
Mark was thirty years old when a routine traffic stop reshaped his life. He had been driving home from a late design meeting, exhausted, his mind still cycling through pixel grids and client revisions. The street was quiet, the hour past midnight, when the flashing blue lights erupted in his rearview mirror. He pulled over, heart already hammering, and reached for his registration as the officer approached. That movement—the fumbling hand reaching toward the glovebox—provoked a violent reaction. The officer shouted, drew his weapon, ordered Mark out of the car. He was thrown to the asphalt, face pressed against the cold ground, hands wrenched behind his back. A small crowd of bystanders had gathered at the corner; Mark could hear their murmurs, their phones held up like silent accusations. In the commotion, someone yelled that Mark had been reaching for a weapon. He hadn't. The officer eventually released him with a warning, but the damage was done.

In the weeks that followed, Mark could not shake the image of the gun barrel or the sensation of asphalt grit against his cheek. He started sleeping poorly, and the dark of his bedroom began to feel like a trap. He would wake at three in the morning, disoriented, drenched in sweat, certain that footsteps were approaching. Nighttime became something to dread rather than simply endure. At first, he tried to push through, but his mind kept returning to that moment. He began to avoid driving altogether, but his job as a graphic designer required him to commute to a downtown office. The subway was worse—crowded platforms and packed cars pressed strangers against him, and each sudden movement in his peripheral vision sent a jolt through his chest. He started taking alternate routes, leaving for work before dawn, and leaving early to beat the crowds. His performance suffered; his supervisor noted that he seemed distracted, that his normally meticulous work had become erratic.

The car that had pulled him over was a standard patrol vehicle, but soon every sedan of that make and color triggered the same visceral response. He would see one at a stoplight and his hands would begin to tremble. On more than one occasion, he found himself pulling into a parking lot, covering his face with both hands, pressing his palms against his eyes as though he could block out the memory. He knew it looked strange; he did not care. What frightened him most was not the memory itself but the certainty that it would happen again—that a uniformed figure would appear and he would be helpless.

To quiet the hypervigilance, Mark turned to alcohol. A glass of wine after work became two, became a bottle. He also began taking an old prescription for an anti-anxiety medication that his doctor had given him years ago, taking it more frequently than intended. The numbness was a relief, even if it came with a fog that made his creative work feel like wading through mud. His marriage, already strained by his withdrawal and irritability, dissolved during the second year. His ex-wife told him she could not live with someone who jumped at every sound and spent his evenings half-drunk. Mark did not argue. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that the officer had seen something dangerous in him, and that others could see it too.

Now, three years after the incident, Mark is sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time. He is on the edge of losing his job—he has missed too many deadlines because he cannot face the commute, and he has started working from home only to find himself unable to concentrate, the bottle on his desk a constant temptation. He still covers his face reflexively whenever a police cruiser passes or a security guard enters his building. He no longer drives at night, and he has cancelled plans with the few friends he has left because the thought of a crowded bar or restaurant is unbearable. What he hopes for, he says quietly, is to stop needing the alcohol just to get through the evening. What he is most afraid of is that this is who he is now.
